rv.q: “Good Bones” has much of Ijames’s signature wit and ease with dialogue, but at times the characters’ exchanges seem to reduce them to perspectives in a debate on class and social change.
The result is mostly engaging if not always convincing. There may be a great play inside Good Bones, but it needs a bit more fleshing out.
An intelligent script, it’s only a minor stumble.
Ijames delves into fascinating topics, and Watson and Davis bring passion and fire to their characters’ respective sides.
Good Bones makes for an engaging hour and 45 minutes that teases out questions of responsibility to the people who nurtured us and the places we grew up in.
The play’s foursome has been expertly cast.
Good Bones brings a fresh coat of paint and perspective to the ongoing discussion of gentrification and the impact sprawling developments have on tight-knit communities.
If “Bones” is lacking in suspense, Mr. Ijames’s piquant wit pokes through, and it’s enhanced by the crisp, knowing direction of Saheem Ali.
But what most moves “Good Bones” forward is not plot or character or argument, but the design.

But unlike “Fat Ham,” for which Ijames rightly won the Pulitzer Prize, “Good Bones” – also directed by Saheem Ali -- often seems simultaneously overstuffed and undercooked, giving audiences both too much to chew on and bones and fat to spit out.
But too often, it feels like an inert clash of perspectives, so afraid of not being clear in its positions that it loses its emotional core.
That's the drama that is missing here.
Respectably, if not memorably, acted, and lacking in sufficiently well-sustained dramatic interest, Good Bones tackles a serious problem but not without suffering a few setbacks in the process.
Ijames’s primary argument in the show was embodied in Carmen— change can be good when you go about it with reverence for the past, mutual respect for your present, and hope for your future.
Under Saheem Ali’s thoughtful direction, the cast is uniformly excellent, maintaining a sense of good will even when the conversations becomes heated.
Ijames has created a powerfully fascinating feast around history and trauma, relationships, and conflicting values, peppered with supernatural laughter and honor.
Good bones, yes, the play does have that, but it is also at times confusing and plodding and feels like it is covered in construction plastic, still awaiting the final reveal.
Even with its occasional skeletal forays, The Hills of California has good bones, filled with a glorious beauty.

cn.t: Ijames' gentrification drama offers provocative themes and a stunning set, but critics find the execution uneven. Praised for strong performances and timely subject matter, yet faulted for feeling underdeveloped and occasionally plodding.

vr.q: this play still grounds its conversations in a reasonably believable plot with pretty developed characters
